title: Let the agent choose what to remember
dek: Anthropic's memory study found that strong models remember best when left to judge what matters, with an offline pass to fix their notes. Plus secrets saved by a convenience button, and a 2004 racing game recompiled for the browser.

theme.mood: a Sunday about what agents keep, and what they should not

tldr.text: Anthropic's memory study: with a memory store, Opus 5.5 rose from 0.655 to 0.838 on a learning benchmark, and telling models to **record only failures** shrank the gain.
An offline "dreaming" pass that rereads transcripts fixed a wrong note that had kept an agent stuck in a Pokémon cave; the corrected run got out.
Apiiro found **1,379 secrets** in 1,122 public copies of Claude Code's local settings file, saved when people approved an exact command once and for all.
A fan project runs Need for Speed: Underground 2 in Chrome by translating the game's x86 code to C ahead of time and compiling it to WebAssembly.
SAG-AFTRA now lets studios hire union actors for pitch demos, as long as under 30% of production funding is secured.

blocks.title: Memory works best when the model picks the notes
blocks.gist: Anthropic tested how AI agents should remember things between sessions. Strong models did best when trusted to decide what to write down, and an offline pass that rereads old logs fixed notes that had gone wrong.
blocks.background: An agent forgets everything when a session ends unless something is saved. Claude Code, the Claude API and Managed Agents all now offer some form of memory.
blocks.takeaway: Tell the agent what memory is for, not what to record, keep the always-loaded part small, and check notes against the original logs. Fixed rules like "only record failures" made memory less useful.
body: In a November 6 post, Anthropic's Lance Martin lays out memory as four layers: raw **transcripts** of what happened, short **notes** the model writes, larger **representations** such as a wiki it maintains, and a small **injected context** loaded into every new session.

The test that frames it is CL-Bench's database task: answer a question, learn the right answer, and leave a note for next time. With a memory store, Opus 5.5 went from 0.655 to 0.838 mean reward and Sonnet 5 from 0.306 to 0.610. Sonnet 4.6 barely moved (0.330 to 0.364) until its instructions were refined. Telling models to record only failures cut the gain: by 0.234 for Opus 5 and 0.150 for Opus 4.7.

The new piece is **dreaming**: between sessions, a process rereads transcripts, corrects notes, builds wiki pages and decides what earns a place in the injected layer. In a Pokémon Red run, an agent wrote down the wrong side of a building, declared the cave done and kept falling off a one-way ledge. After dreaming checked that note against the transcript and rewrote it, the agent went back in and reached the next city at action 1,935; the uncorrected run never did.

stat.label: Opus 5.5's score on a learning benchmark, without and with memory

terms.def: The full, searchable log of everything an agent did and saw in a session.
Text loaded automatically at the start of every session, before the agent does anything.
Anthropic's name for an offline job that reorganises and corrects an agent's memory between sessions.
The average score an agent earns per task on a benchmark, from 0 for failure to 1 for full marks.
A continual learning benchmark that checks whether an agent gets better at a task by remembering past attempts.

deep: Anthropic separates memory from three things it is not: changes to the model's weights, learning from examples in the prompt, and compaction, which swaps old turns for a summary inside one session.

Instruction following decided whether memory helped at all: Sonnet 4.6 read its memory files less than half the time, Sonnet 5 nine times in ten without being asked. With refined instructions Sonnet 4.6 reached 0.641.
Claude Code loads only the first 200 lines or 25 KB of MEMORY.md at session start, so the post treats that file as an index that points to detail elsewhere, not a place to keep everything.
blocks.why: Most agent setups now keep a memory file of some kind. This is the first public measurement of which habits help it and which hurt, across several model generations.
blocks.forYou: Audit the MEMORY.md and CLAUDE.md files across the plugin and SaaS repos: trim each to an index under 200 lines, move detail into linked pages, and drop rules that tell the agent what kind of thing to record. A weekly routine that rereads recent transcripts and fixes notes is the dreaming pattern in miniature.

blocks.title: Same game, 413 memory files against 10
blocks.gist: Two Claude models played Pokémon Red with the freedom to keep notes. The older one filled 413 files and earned one badge; the newer one kept about ten and earned four.
blocks.plain: More notes are not better memory. A model that writes less, and only what it cannot see on screen, finds its way faster.
body: Anthropic drew both memory folders as treemaps at the same scale. Claude Sonnet 3.7 built 225 folders and nearly a million characters, many named like fresh starts ("consolidated", "master", "core") and a few in alarm ("emergency"). Claude Fable 5 kept a locations folder, a gameplay folder and one global.md, about 43,000 characters.
The post's advice from this: do not save what the agent can read off the screen each turn. Save the strategies, plans and tested rules that exist only because the agent worked them out.

image.alt: Two treemaps at the same scale: Sonnet 3.7's memory is a large grid of many folders, several highlighted orange as fresh starts and one red as an emergency folder; Fable 5's is a small block of three items.

terms.def: Charts that draw each folder as a rectangle sized by how much it holds.

blocks.why: It is the clearest picture yet of memory sprawl, and it suggests the fix is fewer, sharper notes rather than a better folder scheme.
blocks.forYou: Game-playing agents for the action RPG's playtests should follow the same rule: store routes and tested tactics, never what the screen already shows.

blocks.title: Six memory habits the experiments back
blocks.gist: The study ends with practical advice for anyone giving an agent memory, each point tied to one of its tests.
blocks.intro: From Anthropic's tests across six models, Pokémon runs and wiki-building tasks:

steps.title: Say what memory is for
steps.text: Explain the goal and let a strong model decide what is worth writing. Fixed rules such as "record only failures" cut the benefit.

steps.title: Keep the top layer small
steps.text: Everything injected costs tokens in every session, and a wrong note there spreads everywhere. Treat it as an index with links.

steps.title: Check notes against logs
steps.text: A wrong note gets trusted later. Reread the transcript before promoting or keeping a claim.

steps.title: Move detail down
steps.text: Push specifics into pages lower in the hierarchy and leave a link behind in the top layer.

steps.title: One page per writer
steps.text: Four agents sharing one table overwrote each other and kept 41 of 57 facts; one page per contract kept all 57.

steps.title: Nudge older models
steps.text: Weaker models need an explicit prompt to read their memory and to test their theories.

blocks.why: These are cheap changes to a memory file or a prompt, and each one comes with a measured effect rather than a hunch.

blocks.title: "Don't ask again" saved passwords into public repos
blocks.gist: When people told Claude Code to stop asking about a command, it saved that exact command, password included, in a project file that many then pushed to GitHub. Researchers found 1,379 secrets that way.
blocks.background: Claude Code asks before running shell commands; "Yes, and don't ask again" writes an allow rule so it stops asking.
blocks.intro: Apiiro searched public GitHub for `.claude/settings.local.json` and found 104,185 copies. Of the 1,122 that held a secret, here is what the two most common secret scanners caught:
blocks.note: Scanners were run without checking whether secrets still work. Misses were mostly passwords typed inside commands, after PGPASSWORD=, sshpass -p or mysql -p.

terms.def: A saved permission that lets an agent run a command without asking you again.
A list of files git ignores on one computer only, unlike a project's .gitignore, which travels with the repository.
Tools that search code for passwords and keys before or after it is published.

deep: Claude Code adds the file to the user's global git excludes on first write, which protects only that machine. It never adds it to the project's .gitignore, so a fresh clone, another machine or a teammate can commit it.

Types found: 379 database passwords, 43 SSH logins to public servers, 42 GitHub, GitLab and npm tokens, 23 AWS keys. Git history holds 734 more secrets in 509 repositories, and 211 forks of 74 repositories carry copies. In 539 of 1,105 traced repositories, a commit co-authored by Claude changed the file.

The Hacker News reports that a related bug report from August 2025 was closed by a bot as "not planned" after 60 days, and that the researchers' reports got no reply. Apiiro reproduced the behaviour with Opus 5.5 and Fable 5.1.
blocks.why: Agent settings folders are now as sensitive as .env files. Approving a pattern instead of an exact command, and keeping secrets in variables, avoids the problem.
blocks.forYou: Check every repo for a tracked .claude/settings.local.json and for exact-command approvals with credentials, especially the Supabase and deploy commands. Today's Try this walks through it.

blocks.title: The agent said it deployed; the containers were a day old
blocks.gist: An agent reported a clean deploy, and every word was true, but it had only pulled the code and never rebuilt, so the new pages returned errors. The fix is to check each claim on the server, outside the agent.
blocks.intro: What the report said, against what the server showed:

rows.right: It ran git pull. No rebuild, no new image.
Running images were 23 hours older than the merge.
The old containers were healthy, so checks passed while new pages returned 404.
Separate checks: server commit equals the expected one, image is newer than it, the readiness URL answers.

blocks.verdict: Ask agents for structured reports (the claim, the exact command, its output, and what was not verified), and run the checks yourself. Commenters suggest stamping the commit hash into the image label and comparing strings, not timestamps.

terms.def: The family of HTTP status codes a server returns when it fails to handle a request.
An address the app answers only once it is fully started and able to serve requests.

blocks.why: Health checks prove that something is running, not that it is the new thing. Any agent that deploys needs its claims checked against the server.
blocks.forYou: Add a post-deploy step to the SaaS routines that compares the running image's commit label with the merged commit and fails loudly when they differ.

blocks.title: A 2004 racing game, recompiled to run in Chrome
blocks.gist: A fan translated every function of Need for Speed: Underground 2's PC code into C, compiled it for the browser and rebuilt the Windows pieces it needs on web technology. You bring your own copy of the game.
blocks.background: The project builds on Talha Müderrisoğlu's NFSU2Recomp, which recompiled the same game for Apple Silicon Macs.

nodes.label: x86 code to C
nodes.note: A Python tool lifts each function of the game's executable into C, ahead of time.

nodes.label: C to WebAssembly
nodes.note: Compiled with wasi-sdk into one module; the game's threads run as workers on shared memory.

nodes.label: Direct3D 9 to WebGPU
nodes.note: The Windows graphics calls are reimplemented on the browser's GPU API.

blocks.caption: Source: the nfsu2-web README. Chrome, and Firefox where it has WebGPU.

A compact code format browsers run at near-native speed.
The modern browser interface for drawing with the graphics card.

deep: The repository is MIT-licensed, has about 1,100 stars, and is not affiliated with EA. It needs one exact SPEED2.EXE (4,800,512 bytes). A Rust server serves the page, the module and your game folder, and connects players for free roam.
It reached the top of Hacker News on November 7 with 872 points. The same tree still builds a native macOS version.
blocks.why: Static recompilation is becoming a practical route to bring old native games to the web, with no emulator in between.
blocks.forYou: Worth a read before any browser build of older C++ code: the runtime folder shows how much of Windows a game really touches.

blocks.title: AMD upscales textures at sample time, with one shared network
blocks.gist: Two AMD researchers store game textures at lower resolution and let a small neural network rebuild detail on the fly whenever the GPU reads a texel, with no training per asset.
blocks.plain: Ship smaller textures, and let one tiny network shared by every material fill in the detail when the shader samples them.
body: Earlier neural texture compression trains a network for each asset, which changes the asset pipeline. Shin Fujieda and Takahiro Harada instead trained one small network on many texture patches, so it works on color, normal and roughness maps it has never seen.

On a hangar scene it beat bicubic and Lanczos filters on perceptual error (0.075 against 0.156 for diffuse color). A per-asset network still scores better, and the authors have not yet measured how long it takes per frame.

image.alt: A rendered sci-fi hangar with a spaceship, with three coloured boxes marking the regions the paper compares up close.

terms.def: One pixel of a texture, the image wrapped onto a 3D surface.
A score of how different two images look to people, rather than pixel by pixel.
A classic, high-quality filter for resizing images.

blocks.why: Texture memory is the first limit on phones and in browsers. A shared upscaler would shrink downloads without touching each asset.
blocks.forYou: A direction to watch for the browser and mobile games and for lighter Fab sample content; not usable until AMD shows frame times or code.

learn.question: What does it mean to statically recompile a game?
learn.answer: It means translating a game's finished machine code into source code for another machine once, ahead of time, then compiling that. An emulator does the translating live, while the game runs.
learn.analogy: An emulator is an interpreter whispering a book to you line by line as you read; static recompilation is a translated edition printed before you open it.
body: A shipped game is machine code for one processor, such as x86 for PCs. To run it elsewhere you either imitate that processor at run time, which costs speed, or translate the code before it runs. Static recompilers walk through the executable, turn each function into equivalent C, and let a normal compiler build it for the new target.
The hard part is everything around the code: the operating system and graphics calls the game expects. Recompilation projects rewrite those layers, so Direct3D calls land on Metal or WebGPU.
N64: Recompiled and XenonRecomp made the approach popular for consoles; today's browser port of Need for Speed: Underground 2 applies it to a PC game and WebAssembly.

diagram.caption: No emulator runs at play time; the translation happened before.

terms.def: The raw numeric instructions a processor executes.
A program that imitates another machine's processor while the software runs.
A tool that turns machine code back into a higher-level language.

tryThis.title: Find the secrets your agent approvals saved
tryThis.gist: Check whether a "don't ask again" approval has put a password into a file your repository tracks, and fix it before it ships.
tryThis.needs: A repository where you use Claude Code, and git.

steps.title: See if the file is tracked
steps.text: In each repository, list tracked agent files and check the local settings file's history (commands below). Any output means it is or was committed.

steps.title: Read the allow rules
steps.text: Open .claude/settings.local.json and .claude/settings.json and look for passwords, tokens or keys inside approved commands.

steps.title: Rotate first
steps.text: If you find a secret that was ever committed, change that password or key before cleaning up; history and forks keep the old one.

steps.title: Untrack and ignore
steps.text: Untrack the local file and add it to the project's own .gitignore, not only your machine's global excludes.

steps.title: Approve patterns
steps.text: Replace exact-command rules with patterns like Bash(npm run:*), and pass secrets as environment variables so rules hold only the name.

code.code:
git ls-files | grep -E '^\.(claude|cursor|gemini)/'
git log --all --oneline -- .claude/settings.local.json

# if it was committed, after rotating the secrets:
git rm --cached .claude/settings.local.json
echo '.claude/settings.local.json' >> .gitignore

tryThis.check: The first two commands print nothing in every repository, and no allow rule contains a literal password or token.

terms.def: Replace a password or key with a new one so the leaked one stops working.

tryThis.forYou: Run it across the Fab plugin repos, the SaaS backends and the routine repos; the Supabase and SSH deploy commands are the likeliest to carry credentials.

lab.title: Trace2Eval: Contextualized Evaluation of Coding Agents from Real-World Traces
lab.headline: Turn real agent sessions into a private test set, and let rubric feedback lift scores by ten points
lab.authors: Ji Shi, Lirong Jie, Lexiao Zou, et al. (Harbin Institute of Technology, Shenzhen)
lab.problem: Public coding benchmarks use tidy tasks and hidden tests, which say little about the messy requests people actually give agents.
lab.idea: Start from 20,000 anonymised real sessions, rebuild each one's original request and starting workspace, rerun a candidate agent, and score the result with human-aligned rubrics and a judge agent. Then give the agent the rubric feedback and let it revise.
lab.result: 129 tasks survived. Across 19 model and harness pairs, one rubric-guided revision added 10.05 points on average, up to 19.28; the judge agreed with human labels 93.0% of the time, as often as humans agreed with each other.
lab.useIt: Replay a handful of your own past agent sessions from their starting commit, write three to five rubric lines each, and use them to compare prompt, skill or model changes on your real work.
lab.forYou: A private regression set from past Claude Code sessions on the plugin repos would show whether a new skill or hook actually helps.

image.alt: Four-step pipeline figure: trace selection from real logs, context recovery with replay and environment tuning, agent execution, and artifact evaluation with rubrics, LLM agents and a judge.

lab.title: Cognitive Tours: Making Understanding a Deliverable in AI-Assisted Development
lab.headline: A map of goals, decisions and code that agent skills audit but only people write
lab.where: arXiv preprint; short version submitted to the ICSE 2027 demo track
lab.problem: When agents write most of the code, teams lose track of why it is the way it is: the goals and reasoning never get written down.
lab.idea: Link waypoints (goals, needs, decisions, code, tests, risks, open questions) to real files, and string them into guided tours with human commentary. Four Claude Code skills read the map and git history to flag stale descriptions and unrecorded work, but never edit the map themselves.
lab.result: A working prototype and a live demo; the paper proposes an evaluation rather than reporting one.
lab.useIt: Borrow the split: let an agent audit your design notes against the code and recent commits, and keep the writing for a person.
lab.forYou: An audit-only skill that flags stale design notes in the plugin repos fits the existing skill setup with little work.

image.alt: The Cognitive Tours app: a graph of colour-coded waypoints such as user needs, decisions and tests, with one AI instruction waypoint highlighted and a tour panel on the right.
